planting.note: Plant a grafted or budded sapling in full sun in spring; stake loosely for the first year since young wood is brittle in wind.

directions: 'Purple Robe' was selected for flower color, producing dense eight-inch, wisteria-like racemes of fragrant rose-purple blossoms in late spring that are showier than the white flowers of the wild species. New leaflets emerge with a coppery-red tint before settling into blue-green summer foliage and clear yellow fall color. As a nitrogen-fixer it thrives in poor, dry, or disturbed soils and grows quickly once established, but the same vigor means root suckers and storm-prone brittle limbs need regular attention. Site it away from patios and walkways where dropped seed pods and thorny sucker growth would be a nuisance.
sources: University of Missouri Extension Lowry Mall Tree Trail

planting.note: Plant grafted stock in full sun to part shade in spring; prune annually in late summer to maintain the twisted branch habit and remove any straight-growing reversion shoots.

directions: Sold under the trademark Twisty Baby, this dwarf sport of black locust twists and curls its branches into a gnarled, almost shrubby silhouette that reads as a landscape oddity in winter when bare. It still produces the fragrant white pea-like flower clusters typical of the species in late spring, followed by yellow fall foliage on the same contorted stems. Growth is far more compact and slower than the species, making it workable near patios where a full-size black locust would not fit, though lower branches can still carry small thorns. It tolerates poor, dry soil and road salt but benefits from an annual tidy-up prune to keep the twisting habit from degrading into a tangled mess.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in full sun in spring; works well spaced tightly as a narrow screen or windbreak element.

directions: 'Sutherland' is a strictly upright, narrow-columnar selection of Siberian peashrub bred for cold-prairie windbreak and screen plantings where width is limited. Small yellow pea-like flowers dangle beneath fine compound foliage in mid-spring, and the foliage turns yellow before dropping in fall, revealing smooth olive-green winter bark. It shrugs off drought, poor rocky soil, and heavy winter cold once established, asking for little beyond an open, sunny spot. Because it stays so slender, it can be set closer together than the species for a quick vertical hedge effect without the typical peashrub sprawl.

planting.note: Plant a grafted sapling in full sun to light shade in spring; the narrow vase shape fits tight urban or street-side planting strips.

directions: Sold under the trade name Ruby Vase, this Persian ironwood selection grows in a distinctly upright, vase-shaped form that is noticeably narrower than the broad-spreading species, making it a better fit for confined sites. New spring leaves emerge ruby-red along the margins before maturing to glossy dark green for summer, then turning outstanding orange-red and gold in fall. Tiny red, petal-less flowers appear on bare branches in late winter, and mature trunks develop the same exfoliating gray-and-tan patchwork bark prized on the straight species. It adapts to a range of soils in full sun with regular moisture and shows good resistance to the pests and disease problems that trouble many other street trees.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in full sun to part sun in well-drained soil; flowers on old wood, so prune for shape only right after bloom.

directions: Bred at North Carolina State University and sold under the trademark Snow Day Blizzard, this pearlbush selection carries flowers roughly twice the size of the older 'The Bride' cultivar, opening from round pearl-like buds strung along pendant stems in early spring. The pure-white bloom display is dense enough to hide the stems entirely for a week or two each year. Habit is rounded and shrubbier than the taller species, filling out to a broad, dense mound that needs no support staking. It tolerates average garden soil and short dry spells once established but performs best with consistent moisture through its spring growth flush.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant a young balled-and-burlapped or container tree in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil; seed needs scarification and cold stratification before it will germinate reliably.

directions: This East Asian relative of the better-known American yellowwood bears fragrant white pea-shaped flowers with a faint yellow throat flush in upright clusters from late spring into early summer, somewhat later and more reliably than Cladrastis kentukea. Compound leaves of seven to eleven oval leaflets turn a clean bright yellow in fall before dropping from smooth gray bark and brittle, easily broken twigs. It prefers a sheltered site out of strong wind because of that brittleness and performs best in deep, moderately moist soil rather than extremes of wet or dry. Give it room to develop its broad, dome-shaped crown since it resents crowding and transplants best while still young.

planting.note: Plant a grafted sapling in full sun in spring; tolerates urban soil, heat, and road salt once established.

directions: Selected at North Dakota State University for superior cold hardiness, 'Harve' is a thornless and seedless honeylocust marketed as Northern Acclaim that avoids both the vicious thorns of the wild species and the messy pods of seeded cultivars. Fine-textured compound leaves cast dappled rather than dense shade, allowing lawn and underplantings to thrive beneath it, and foliage turns golden yellow in fall. Its upright, symmetrical crown broadens gracefully with age into a pyramidal shade tree well suited to streets, parking areas, and other tough urban sites. It shows good resistance to the canker disease that can afflict other honeylocust selections and tolerates drought once its root system is established.
